The advertisement constructs freedom as escape from the noise and obligations of adult working life, a freedom that can be recovered through purchase.

The headline does this immediately: "Somewhere out there, your phone has no signal." The expected anxiety is reversed by the one-word sentence "Good.", which positions disconnection as a luxury. The image reinforces this, a car "parked alone on a salt lake at dawn" in which "No people are visible", so freedom is figured as solitude and emptiness.

The body copy then frames freedom as something the reader has lost. The second-person address and parallel sentences "Maybe you were nine, and the creek was the whole world. Maybe you were nineteen, and the road was." invoke nostalgia, while the terse "Then life got busy. Then it got loud." compresses adulthood into a decline. The car is offered as restitution, "built for the moment you take it back", where the verb implies that freedom is a possession to be reclaimed.

Even technical features are translated into this idea. The fuel range means "the next servo is a suggestion, not a plan", converting a specification into spontaneity, and the quiet cabin lets you "finally hear yourself think", with a playful aside, "(We checked. You have some good ideas.)", that flatters the reader. Personification sharpens the contrast with office life: "The salt doesn't care about your inbox."

Finally, the imperatives "Go further. Come back different." and the tagline "Built for the long way round." present freedom as transformation, but on a round trip. The freedom constructed is temporary, safe and purchasable: an escape that always returns home.

questions.model:
At a literal level the advertisement repeatedly contradicts its promise of escape, but these contradictions are not failures of the copy; they reveal what it is really selling, which is the feeling of escape without its risks. The extent of contradiction is therefore great, yet strategically managed.

The promise is extravagant. The headline celebrates having "no signal", and the copy claims that "Out there, nobody asks what you do for a living." Yet the same copy reassures the reader that connection is never far away: "when you need the world again, it's right there". The list that follows, "12.3-inch touchscreen, wireless smartphone mirroring, and a satellite emergency beacon", reinstalls the very devices the headline rejected. The claim that "freedom is better when someone knows where you are" is a paradox that admits the audience does not want true isolation; it wants solitude with a safety net.

The fine print deepens the contradiction. The range that made servos "a suggestion" is "based on laboratory testing", and the claim that the car "reads the ground before you do" sits awkwardly beside the warning that off-road driving suits only "experienced drivers on legally accessible tracks". Most strikingly, the central image is undone: "Do not drive on salt lakes; vehicle shown on a closed set." The wilderness was staged. Even safety becomes an ongoing payment, since the beacon "requires an active subscription after 12 months".

However, these contradictions do not necessarily weaken the advertisement. Fine print is designed to be skimmed, and the warm second-person voice and nostalgic appeals do their emotional work before the reader reaches the qualifications. Moreover, the audience the copy flatters, professionals who can afford "$78,990", may knowingly accept a curated, temporary escape: "Go further. Come back different" promises return as well as departure.

The advertisement thus contradicts its promise almost completely in fact, while sustaining it in feeling. A critical reader recognises that the product is not freedom but a reassuring image of it.

sets.title: It's Not Cold
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original eulogy, delivered by a former swimmer at the funeral of a swimming-pool coach in a country town. The speaker, the coach and the town of Yarrumba are fictional.
sets.body:
Lorna Pike taught half this town to swim, and she taught the other half to stop complaining about the cold.

If you grew up in Yarrumba, you know the sound I mean: a whistle at six in the morning, so loud the magpies left the pool fence, and a voice behind it saying, 'It's not cold. You're just not moving yet.' I heard that sentence four hundred times between the ages of seven and seventeen. I believed it about twice.

Lorna ran the pool for thirty-one summers. She opened it in October, when the water was still green at the deep end, and she closed it in March, when the last of us had stopped turning up. In between she ran learn-to-swim for the toddlers, squad for the keen kids, aqua aerobics for the ladies from the CWA, and a Tuesday night session for adults who had never learned and were too embarrassed to say so. She never told anyone who came to the Tuesday nights. Some of them are here today. You know who you are. She kept your secret, and so will I.

She was not a soft woman. She would tell you your tumble turn looked like a dropped wardrobe. She would tell your parents, too. But if you were the kid whose family couldn't pay for the season pass, you would find, somehow, that your name was already on the list, and if you asked about it she would look at you as if you'd said something in Latin.

I want to tell you about one morning. I was twelve, and I had come last in the district carnival by the length of a whole pool, and I had decided I was finished with swimming forever. I sat in the change rooms in my towel and would not come out. Lorna didn't come in after me. She just stood outside the door and talked about the weather for twenty minutes, the drought, the price of chlorine, the new council, until I came out because I was bored. Then she handed me a kickboard and said, 'Two laps. Nobody's watching.' Nobody was. It was the best swim of my life.

That was her method. She didn't fix you. She waited beside you until you were ready to move, and then she made sure you had something to hold on to.

The council has asked me to say that the pool will be renamed in her honour, and I'm glad. But I think Lorna would want something harder than a sign. She would want the pool open in October, green water and all. She would want the Tuesday nights to keep going. She would want somebody standing on the edge at six in the morning with a whistle and a terrible joke, telling some shivering kid it's not cold.

So here is what I am asking. If she taught you, teach someone. If she kept your secret, keep somebody else's. And when you go past the pool this summer and hear that whistle, and you will hear it, whoever is blowing it, get in.

It's not cold. You're just not moving yet.

The speaker transforms Lorna's catchphrase from a remembered joke into a principle for living, and finally into an instruction to the grieving community, so that the speech ends by letting Lorna's voice speak again.

The phrase first appears as comic characterisation. Set against "a whistle at six in the morning, so loud the magpies left the pool fence", the line "It's not cold. You're just not moving yet." captures Lorna's brisk, unsentimental toughness, and the speaker's hyperbolic aside, "I heard that sentence four hundred times between the ages of seven and seventeen. I believed it about twice.", invites shared laughter from listeners who heard it too.

The change-room anecdote then reveals the philosophy inside the joke. The speaker distils Lorna's method in short declaratives: "She didn't fix you. She waited beside you until you were ready to move". The verb "move" links directly to the catchphrase: discomfort is not denied, but it is overcome by action rather than by rescue.

In the final section the phrase becomes a call to action. The anaphora of "She would want" builds a picture of a living memorial, "something harder than a sign", and the parallel imperatives "If she taught you, teach someone. If she kept your secret, keep somebody else's." convert gratitude into obligation. The blunt command "get in." applies the old poolside instruction to the whole community.

Finally, the speaker repeats the catchphrase as her closing line. Its meaning has expanded: the cold is now grief, and moving means continuing Lorna's work. The circular structure lets the speech end in Lorna's own words, so that she both comforts and challenges the mourners one last time.

sets.title: Figures Do Not Have Names
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: Text 1 is an original speech written in the style of the early 1930s, when many Australians were unemployed during the Great Depression; the speaker is fictional. Text 2 is an original feature article extract about a food-delivery rider; the rider, the journalist and the platform are fictional.
sets.body:
Speech at a meeting of the unemployed, the Domain, Sydney, 1931

Friends, and I call you friends, for there is no other word for men who have stood in the same queue since daylight:

They tell us that there is no work. I say there is work enough in this city for every pair of hands in this park. There are roads unmade and houses unbuilt and children unfed, and there are men here who can make and build and feed, and the only thing that stands between the two is a ledger in a bank in Pitt Street.

They tell us to be patient. We have been patient. We were patient in the trenches, where we were told we were fighting for a better world. We were patient at the wharves and in the shearing sheds, where we were told the good times were coming. Patience, friends, is a fine virtue in a man with a full belly. In a man with hungry children it begins to look very like surrender.

They tell us that we are a burden. Look about you. Look at the man beside you. That man laid the bricks of the very building where they tell him he is a burden. That man's hands drove the rivets of the bridge they are so proud of. There is not a stone in this city that was not lifted by somebody's father.

I do not ask for charity. Charity is what is given to a man you have decided is less than yourself. I ask for work, and wages for work, and the plain respect that is owed to any man who will put his back to a load.

And I say this to the gentlemen in their offices, who will read of this meeting in tomorrow's papers: you may count us as figures in your columns. But figures do not stand in the rain. Figures do not have names. Every man here has a name, and before this winter is out, by God, you shall learn some of them.

pair.title: The App Doesn't Know His Name
pair.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
pair.body:
It is 9.40 pm on a Friday in Parramatta, and Arjun has been riding since eleven this morning. His phone is clamped to the handlebars of a second-hand e-bike, and every few minutes it chimes, a bright, cheerful sound, like a game show contestant getting an answer right. Each chime is an offer: a burger, four kilometres, $6.80. He has fifteen seconds to accept.

'If you say no too many times,' he says, 'it stops asking.'

Arjun is twenty-six. In Hyderabad he studied civil engineering. Here, he is what the platform calls an independent contractor, which means he supplies the bike, the phone, the insurance and the body, and the app supplies the work, when it chooses to. He doesn't have a manager. He has a rating: 4.91 out of five. He knows the number the way other people know their height.

Nobody has ever been rude to him, exactly. That is part of the strangeness. The customers he delivers to mostly don't look at him at all; they take the bag at the door with their eyes on a screen, or they have left instructions to leave it on the mat and not to knock. Once, a woman in Westmead came out to the gate in her dressing gown with a glass of water, because it was thirty-eight degrees. He still talks about her. He doesn't know her name either.

The platform, in a statement, said that riders 'value the flexibility' of the work and that its pay model 'reflects market conditions'. Both of these things may be true. Arjun does value the flexibility; it lets him study for his engineering accreditation in the mornings. And the market conditions are certainly reflected, in the way a puddle reflects the sky.

At 10.15 the chime comes again. A bubble tea, two kilometres, $5.20. He taps accept before I can ask whether it's worth it.

'Everything is worth it,' he says, pulling his helmet on, 'until you add it up.'

Then he is gone into the traffic, a small green light among the red ones, and somewhere a restaurant tablet is already printing his first name.

questions.text: Compare how Text 1 and Text 2 represent the dignity of work and what threatens it.

questions.model:
Both texts insist that work carries a dignity that is threatened when people are reduced to numbers, but they locate the threat differently. Text 1 confronts a system that withholds work from people who want it; Text 2 examines a system that supplies work while withholding recognition. Read together, they suggest that dignity depends less on employment itself than on being known.

Both texts set names against figures. The speaker in Text 1 warns the "gentlemen in their offices" that "figures do not stand in the rain. Figures do not have names", and his closing threat that "you shall learn some of them" asserts identity as a form of power. Text 2 shows the figures winning: Arjun has "a rating: 4.91 out of five" instead of a manager, and the article closes on a tablet printing only "his first name". Even his one moment of human connection ends with "He doesn't know her name either."

Both texts also locate power in distant, abstract systems. Text 1's "ledger in a bank in Pitt Street" anticipates Text 2's app, which supplies work "when it chooses to". Each text exposes official language: the speaker mocks the refrain "They tell us", while the journalist quotes the platform's claim that riders "value the flexibility" and undercuts its "market conditions" with the ironic simile "in the way a puddle reflects the sky".

The texts differ most in voice and response. Text 1 is collective and oratorical: its inclusive "we", its demand for "work, and wages for work, and the plain respect", and its oath "by God" rouse a crowd to action. Text 2 is quiet and individual. Arjun is an "independent contractor" who rides alone, and his aphorism "Everything is worth it... until you add it up" registers weary calculation rather than defiance. Notably, Text 1's dignity belongs only to "men", while Text 2 finds its one moment of grace in a woman at a gate.

Together, the texts suggest that work and wages are not sufficient without the third term the 1931 speaker named: respect, which in both eras depends on being seen as a person rather than counted as a figure.

sets.title: Visiting Hours
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original short scene from a play. Dana and Michael are adult siblings waiting while their father is in surgery. They have not spoken for eleven years. A header is a grain harvester.
sets.body:
A family room in a regional hospital, late at night. A vending machine hums. Two vinyl chairs with an empty one between them, a box of tissues, a television mounted high on the wall with the sound off. DANA, forty, in work clothes, sits very upright with her handbag on her knees. MICHAEL, thirty-six, in a football jumper, enters with two cups of machine coffee. He holds one out. She looks at it.

MICHAEL: White, no sugar. (Beat.) Or has that changed too?

DANA: It's fine. (She takes it. She does not drink.)

MICHAEL: (sitting, leaving one chair between them) Nurse said another hour. Maybe two.

DANA: I spoke to the surgeon.

MICHAEL: Course you did.

DANA: Someone had to.

(Pause. On the television, silent, a man points at a weather map.)

MICHAEL: He asked for you. Before they took him down. He said, 'Is Dana coming?'

DANA: (a fraction too fast) And what did you say?

MICHAEL: I said you were on your way.

DANA: I was.

MICHAEL: Eleven years is a long way.

(DANA puts the coffee down on the floor, carefully, as if it might go off.)

DANA: You don't get to do that. You were here. You got to be here.

MICHAEL: Got to.

DANA: Yes, got to. You got the farm, and the ute, and the Sunday roasts, and him telling everyone at the pub how you'd turned the place around —

MICHAEL: I got the overdraft. I got him falling off the header in August because he wouldn't let me drive it. I got him calling me by your name when the sugar was low.

(Silence. DANA looks at him for the first time.)

DANA: My name?

MICHAEL: Dana, get the gate. Dana, where's the — (He stops.) Three, four times a week. Like you'd just gone into town.

(DANA picks up the coffee again. She holds it with both hands.)

DANA: He never rang.

MICHAEL: Neither did you.

DANA: I wrote. At Christmas. I wrote every Christmas.

MICHAEL: I know. They're in the dresser. (Beat.) He opened them. He just didn't know what you wanted him to say.

DANA: Sorry. I wanted him to say sorry.

MICHAEL: (quietly) Yeah. Well. He's not a sorry kind of bloke. He's more of a get-the-gate kind of bloke.

(Something that is almost a laugh escapes DANA. She covers her mouth. MICHAEL moves, slowly, into the empty chair between them. Neither speaks. On the television, the weather map shows rain moving in from the west.)

DANA: That'll be good for the crop.

MICHAEL: Yeah. It will.

(The lights fade slowly as they watch the silent screen.)

Michael's flat echo, "Got to.", repeated as a fragment, questions her assumption, and Dana's insistence, "Yes, got to", leads into a list of what she imagines he gained: "the farm, and the ute, and the Sunday roasts". The parallel structure shows that the siblings share a grammar of grievance but have filled it with opposite content. questions.model:
The scene dramatises reconciliation not as a resolution but as a shift in where the siblings look and sit. It moves from guarded hostility, through a revelation that changes Dana's understanding of the past, to a shared silence in which the conflict is suspended rather than settled.

The opening establishes conflict through clipped, barbed dialogue. Michael's "Or has that changed too?" turns an offer of coffee into an accusation, and his sarcastic "Course you did." answers Dana's competence with resentment; her reply, "Someone had to.", implies that he is less capable. The silent television, on which "a man points at a weather map", underlines their failure to communicate.

The turning point comes through revelation. Michael's disclosure that their father called him "by your name when the sugar was low" stops the argument, and the direction "DANA looks at him for the first time" marks the shift from defensiveness to attention. His broken-off imitation, "Dana, get the gate. Dana, where's the", shows that the father's love was expressed in the language of daily work. Dana's "Sorry. I wanted him to say sorry." is the scene's most exposed moment, and Michael's dry reply that their father is "not a sorry kind of bloke" turns grief into a shared joke. The direction that "Something that is almost a laugh escapes DANA" captures how tentative the connection is.

Staging then does what dialogue cannot. Michael "moves, slowly, into the empty chair between them", closing the gap established at the start, and the fact that "Neither speaks" suggests that silence, once a weapon, has become a space they can share.

The ending is deliberately understated. Dana's "That'll be good for the crop." is her first sentence in the language of the farm and of their father, and Michael's "Yeah. It will." accepts it. The rain "moving in from the west" offers hope, but it remains on a silent screen, and the father's surgery is unresolved. The reconciliation is real, yet fragile: a beginning rather than an ending.

sets.title: Review: The Counting Season
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original book review of a fictional novel. The novel, its author and the reviewer are invented. The Newell Highway is an inland road in New South Wales.
sets.body:
There is a kind of novel that announces itself as important in its first sentence and then spends three hundred pages trying to live up to the announcement. Lena Marchetti's debut is not that kind of novel. The Counting Season begins with a girl counting the cars that pass her family's service station on the Newell Highway, and for a long time it seems content to keep counting. This is its great strength and, eventually, its problem.

The girl is Bianca, fourteen, and the year is 1998. Her father has stopped speaking, not out of anger, the novel is careful to tell us, but because 'the words had worn out, the way a tyre wears out, from the inside where you can't see it'. Bianca's mother runs the station, the till, the roadhouse kitchen and the family's silence with the same tired efficiency. Nothing much happens. A truck driver leaves a book behind. A cousin visits from Griffith. A dog goes missing and comes back.

Marchetti's prose is remarkable for what it refuses to do. It refuses to explain. It refuses, almost entirely, to describe the father's illness in clinical terms; instead we see it the way Bianca sees it, through objects: his reading glasses folded on the windowsill for a whole season, the newspaper still in its plastic sleeve. These chapters have the patience of a long drive, and like a long drive they produce in the reader a strange, receptive calm in which the smallest event, a magpie on a bowser, becomes luminous.

The trouble arrives in the final forty pages, when the novel seems to lose its nerve. Having trusted silence for so long, Marchetti suddenly gives the father a lengthy speech at a family dinner in which he explains himself, his war, his marriage and his regrets, in complete and grammatical paragraphs. It is beautifully written. It is also, I think, a mistake. After three hundred pages teaching us to read what is not said, we are handed everything, and the effect is less like revelation than like the radio coming on too loud in a quiet car.

Still, it would be churlish to let an ending outweigh a book this assured. Marchetti has a gift for the overlooked: for the inland, the in-between, the people who serve you petrol and do not expect to be remembered. The Counting Season is a debut of real distinction, flawed in the way that ambitious first novels often are, by not quite trusting its own best instincts.

Read it slowly. Then argue with the ending.

Four stars.

sets.title: Ghazal for the City I Am Leaving
sets.author: Original text (HSC Companion)
sets.headnote: This is an original ghazal, a form from Arabic, Persian and Urdu poetry made of self-contained couplets. In this version every couplet ends with the same word, and in the final couplet the poet addresses herself by name, as ghazal poets traditionally do. The poet, Ayesha, is fictional. Auburn, Granville, Harris Park and Blacktown are suburbs of western Sydney.
sets.body:
I have packed the kettle and the good knives. It takes a year to leave.
The jacarandas will flower without me. They have never learned to leave.

At Circular Quay the ferries shoulder in and out like patient cattle.
Only the wake behind them, widening, rehearses how to leave.

My mother crossed two oceans with one suitcase and a tin of seeds.
She grew curry leaves in Blacktown. She said you never wholly leave.

Each room goes back to being a room once the pictures are down.
The nail holes stare like questions I forgot to ask. And still I leave.

My friends say, You'll be back, the way you wish a swimmer luck
at the edge of the surf: half blessing, half permission to leave.

My grandfather kept the key to a house across a border he never crossed again.
I have the key now. It opens nothing. It is how we learned to leave.

This city never asked me to belong. It simply let me stay.
That is the kindness of large cities: they make it easy to leave.

From the plane I will try to name the suburbs by their lights,
Auburn, Granville, Harris Park, and lose them one by one, and leave.

Ayesha, when they ask you over there where you are from,
say the name of a city that taught you how to leave.

questions.model: Ending every couplet with "leave" makes departure the poem's inescapable destination: however each couplet begins, it is drawn back to the same word, just as the speaker's thoughts keep returning to the act of going. The refrain also gathers shifting meanings. In "It takes a year to leave" it suggests slow, practical effort; in "you never wholly leave" it implies that leaving is impossible; and in "It is how we learned to leave" it becomes a family inheritance. Because ghazal couplets are self-contained, the refrain is what binds them, so repetition creates unity from fragments, mirroring a speaker trying to hold scattered memories together as she goes.

questions.model: The poet represents leaving as an inheritance passed down through generations, each of whom carries something material that stands for what cannot be carried. The mother "crossed two oceans with one suitcase and a tin of seeds"; the seeds symbolise a culture transplanted rather than abandoned, and the specific, suburban result, "She grew curry leaves in Blacktown", shows heritage taking root in a new place. Her saying, "you never wholly leave", offers one family lesson: that origins persist. The grandfather's key offers a darker one. He kept it for "a house across a border he never crossed again", an image of displacement and loss, and the speaker's flat, short sentences, "I have the key now. It opens nothing.", convey the inheritance of a grief that has no practical use but cannot be discarded. The couplet's conclusion, "It is how we learned to leave", suggests that leaving has become a family skill, almost a tradition. By placing her own departure within these generations, the speaker presents herself as continuing a pattern, though, unlike her grandfather, she leaves by choice.

questions.model:
The poem suggests that belonging is not simply granted by a place or ended by leaving it; it is made through attention, memory and inheritance, and it is often understood most fully at the moment of departure.

First, the poem distinguishes between being permitted to stay and belonging. The speaker observes that "This city never asked me to belong. It simply let me stay." The distinction is ambivalent: the city's indifference is called "the kindness of large cities", because it imposes no demands, yet the same quality makes it "easy to leave". Belonging, the poem implies, requires more than tolerance.

Second, the poem shows that belonging is constructed by people rather than by place. The mother makes Blacktown a home by growing "curry leaves" from her "tin of seeds", so belonging is cultivated, literally rooted, through care. Her claim that "you never wholly leave" suggests that places also persist in those who leave them, an idea reinforced by the grandfather's key, which "opens nothing" yet is still kept. Belonging can outlast the place it refers to.

Third, the act of leaving intensifies the speaker's attachment. The ordinary details she lists, "the kettle and the good knives", the "nail holes" that stare "like questions I forgot to ask", and the litany of suburbs, "Auburn, Granville, Harris Park", show a love expressed through precise naming. Yet the image of losing the suburbs "one by one" from the plane suggests that this belonging is fragile and dependent on memory.

The final couplet draws these ideas together. Addressing herself as "Ayesha", the speaker imagines being asked where she is from and tells herself to "say the name of a city that taught you how to leave." The paradox is the poem's central insight: Sydney's gift is not permanence but the capacity to carry a place within one's identity. Belonging, then, is portable and inherited, like the seeds and the key: never wholly left, never wholly kept.
